summary: Describes procedures for node protection of P2MP and MP2MP LSPs built by mLDP. The point of local repair learns the merge points of a node so it can redirect traffic if that node fails.

plainLanguage.summary: If a bridge goes out, there is a plan for a detour around it.

questions: how to protect p2mp lsps from node failure
what is a point of local repair
what is a merge point in mpls
how does mldp recover from node failure
subtitle: How a multicast MPLS tree can switch to pre-built detours the moment a router on it fails.

tldr.problem: If a router on a multicast label switched path built by mLDP fails, traffic to everything downstream of it stops until the network reconverges.
tldr.mechanism: The protected node tells its downstream neighbours (Merge Points) who the upstream router (Point of Local Repair) is. Each Merge Point opens a targeted LDP session to that router, and the router redirects traffic over pre-established point-to-point LSPs that bypass the failed node.
tldr.outcome: Traffic can be redirected around a failed node without waiting for the tree to be rebuilt. It requires the Point of Local Repair, Merge Points and protected node to support the new capability, and the protected node must be directly connected to both.

sections.title: Protecting a Node on a Multicast LSP
sections.content:
RFC 7715 describes node protection for Point-to-Multipoint and Multipoint-to-Multipoint Label Switched Paths (P2MP and MP2MP LSPs) that were built by the Multipoint Label Distribution Protocol (mLDP, RFC 6388).

To protect a node N, the Point of Local Repair (PLR) of N must learn the Merge Point (MPT) routers of N. Traffic is then redirected to them if N fails. The redirection depends on existing point-to-point LSPs that start at the PLR, end at the MPTs and bypass N. How those LSPs are set up is out of scope, though the RFC mentions techniques based on RSVP-TE or LDP Loop-Free Alternate.

The solution uses a Targeted LDP (tLDP) session between each MPT and the PLR. The RFC says this means no extra procedures are needed for Make-Before-Break, Graceful Restart and Typed Wildcard FEC, at the price of extra tLDP sessions.
sections.plainLanguage: Trucks normally drive through a town, called N. The road crew builds detours ahead of time that skip the town, and the trucks use them only if the town is closed.

sections.title: Finding the PLR
sections.content:
An MPT must first learn who the PLR is. It is the protected node N that advertises the PLR address to its downstream members. When N is not the root, the PLR is the upstream LDP peer, found with the usual mLDP rule for choosing an upstream router toward the root. N MUST advertise that address to a downstream member only if that member has announced support for node protection.

The procedures require the protected node to be directly connected to the PLR and the MPT nodes. The reason given is that mLDP relies on unicast routing, which by default knows only the next hop. Non-directly connected PLR and MPT nodes are out of scope.

When N is the root of an MP2MP LSP, there is no upstream router and no single PLR. Instead the directly connected members all act as both PLR and MPT. N sends each member a list of the other members, so LSR2 would be told {LSR3, LSR1}. The RFC notes this does not replace Root Node Redundancy from RFC 6388, because a new root must still be elected so that new MP2MP LSPs can be created.
sections.plainLanguage: The town tells the drivers on the far side which road crew helper is waiting just before the town. If the town is the very center of the map, every neighbour helps every other neighbour.

sections.title: The New Status Value Elements
sections.content:
The PLR address travels in an LDP Notification message, inside an MP Status TLV, as a new PLR Status Value Element (Type 2). It holds an address family, a count of PLR entries (Num PLR entry) and the entries. Each entry has an A bit (0 means withdraw, 1 means add), 15 reserved bits that MUST be zero on transmit, and the PLR address. An entry is 6 octets for an IPv4 address and 18 octets for an IPv6 address.

To remove all PLR addresses of one address family, N sends a PLR Status Value Element with no entries and Num PLR entry set to zero. The message MUST also carry an MP FEC TLV so the receiver can tie the status to the right LSP.

Going the other way, the MPT tells the PLR which node is protected using a Protected Node Status Value Element (Type 3). It carries an address family and the node address, and its length is 6 octets for IPv4 or 18 octets for IPv6. It rides in a Status TLV with the FEC Label Mapping the MPT sends over the tLDP session.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two little notes. One says who the helper is. The other, sent back to the helper, says which town they are covering for.

sections.title: Using the tLDP Session
sections.content:
A router that receives a PLR Status with PLR addresses becomes an MPT for node protection. If it does not already have one, it MUST set up a tLDP session with each learned PLR address using RFC 7060.

For each protected FEC, the MPT creates a secondary upstream router, the PLR, and assigns it a second label. So the FEC ends up with two local labels: one for the normal upstream node N and one for the PLR. The label mapping sent to the PLR carries the Protected Node Status so the PLR knows what it is for.

The PLR uses that label binding only once the advertised node becomes unreachable. For MP2MP LSPs, the matching upstream binding on the MPT also MUST only be used once N is unreachable. How unreachability is detected is a local decision; the RFC suggests link failure or Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD).
sections.plainLanguage: Each helper gets a secret key to a detour gate. The gate stays locked until the town is really closed.

sections.title: Link Failure Versus Node Failure
sections.content:
When the PLR sees N become unreachable, it cannot tell whether the link or the node failed. The RFC's example also has link protection through a backup node M using Fast Reroute (RFC 4090). The PLR MAY use link protection and node protection at the same time. If only the link failed, the MPTs would then receive packets twice.

To avoid duplicates, an MPT accepts packets from either the primary upstream node N or the secondary upstream PLR, but never both. While N is reachable, the MPT keeps using N. Once N is unreachable, the LSPs from the secondary PLR are activated.

  • Node failure: the MPTs switch to the PLR binding and disable the binding to N.
  • Link failure: N is still reachable, so the MPTs keep N as primary and drop the node-protection traffic. N reconverges and removes the PLR address, and the MPTs MUST send a Label Withdraw to the PLR, which answers with a Label Release.
sections.plainLanguage: Two helpers may both send a truck. The receiver only unloads one of them, so nothing is delivered twice.

sections.title: Capabilities and Cleanup
sections.content:
After the network reconverges, each MPT finds a new best path to the root. They SHOULD use Make-Before-Break from RFC 6388 to move to the new primary upstream node, then MUST send a Label Withdraw to the old upstream router. The tLDP session MAY be torn down when it is no longer needed. The RFC RECOMMENDS a delay first, to avoid the session flapping if the link is flapping.

Support is announced with one new capability, the MP Node Protection Capability (Type 0x0972, Length 2), using the LDP Capabilities mechanism of RFC 5561. Its P bit says the sender can act as PLR and its M bit says it can act as MPT. A PLR sends it to its downstream peers, an MPT sends it to its upstream peer, and a router that can do both sets both bits. The protected node advertises nothing. It sends PLR information to a downstream router only if the PLR signalled PLR capability and the downstream router signalled MPT capability.
sections.plainLanguage: Everyone wears a badge saying whether they can be a helper, a receiver, or both. The town only passes on the helper list when the badges match.

sections.title: Security and IANA Considerations
sections.content:
The procedures add two new TLVs to existing LDP messages. They can be protected by the mechanisms used for LDP messages in RFC 6388 and RFC 5920. The RFC notes that a successful attack could induce a PLR or MPT to support a large number of tLDP sessions and an even larger number of LSPs. An implementation could count them and log a message to the operator if a threshold is crossed.

IANA allocated value 2 (PLR Status Value Element) and value 3 (Protected Node Status Value Element) in the LDP MP Status Value Element type registry. It also allocated the capability TLV code point 0x0972 (MP Node Protection Capability).
sections.plainLanguage: A bad guy could ask the helpers to hold too many keys. The helpers can count the keys and shout if there are too many.
